analysis.one_liner: Caps steel imports at pre-1997 levels for five years and funds steelworker retiree health care with a new steel tax.
analysis.headline: A steel-industry rescue bill backed by 228 House cosponsors — a majority of the chamber, from both parties — never received a vote in any committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the President to roll steel imports back to the levels of the mid-1990s using quotas or tariffs for five years. It would have created a federal trust fund, paid for by a new 1.5% tax on all steel sold, to cover most of the retiree health benefits owed to laid-off and retired steelworkers. It would also have expanded a federal loan guarantee program for struggling steel companies tenfold and offered up to $500 million in grants to companies that merged, on condition they kept most of the workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Steelworkers and retired steelworkers would gain the most directly: the bill would have paid 75% of the cost of retiree health benefits out of a new federal trust fund, rescuing benefits that companies going broke had abandoned. Steel producers would have gained a protected market through quotas, easier access to billions in federally guaranteed loans, and grants covering the environmental cleanup costs of mergers. Steel communities dependent on mill jobs would have gained job protection for five years.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the President, within 60 days, to impose quotas, tariff surcharges, or negotiated export restraint agreements so that steel imports stay at or below average monthly levels from the 36 months before July 1997, with Customs empowered to turn away shipments above the allowed levels, for five years.

It creates a Steelworker Retiree Health Care Trust Fund that pays 75% of qualified retiree health benefit costs for designated steelworker group health plans, funded by a new 1.5% excise tax on steel sold by manufacturers, producers, and importers.

It raises the Emergency Steel Loan Guarantee program ceiling from $1 billion to $10 billion, lifts the per-company limit from $250 million to $500 million, and guarantees up to 95% of a loan, with the board required to act on applications within 45 days.

It authorizes $500 million in grants — up to $100 million per company — for firms that acquire steel producers, to cover environmental compliance costs, but only if the merger keeps at least 80% of steel-production jobs and capacity, with escalating forfeitures if those levels slip.

analysis.who_pays: Every buyer of steel — automakers, appliance makers, builders, and ultimately consumers — would pay more, both because import quotas restrict the cheaper supply and because of the new 1.5% tax added to the price of steel sold. Taxpayers would carry the risk on up to $10 billion in loan guarantees to weak companies and would fund the merger grants. Foreign steel producers and their workers would lose access to the U.S. market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Steel buyers, taxpayers, and foreign exporters

drawbacks.text: Import quotas and the 1.5% excise tax would raise the price of steel for every downstream industry and consumer; steel-using manufacturers employ far more people than steelmaking does, so the cost would fall on a much larger group of workers and shoppers than the bill helps.

The loan guarantee expansion puts federal taxpayers behind up to $10 billion in debt of struggling steel companies, and the merger grants would use public money to subsidize buyouts, with the bill wagering that job-retention penalties are enough to protect the investment.

Across-the-board quotas ignore whether any specific imports are fairly traded, and restricting imports removes the price pressure that pushes high-cost domestic producers to modernize — a cost to consumers with no guarantee the protected industry becomes competitive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The retiree health provision is the strongest part: it would have rescued health benefits for people who worked a lifetime in the mills and saw them vanish when their employers collapsed. But the price is broad and blunt — quotas and a sales tax on steel raise costs for every steel-using business and household, and the loan guarantees and merger subsidies shift company risk onto taxpayers. An honest reading is that the bill trades a modest, real gain for a concentrated group of workers and companies against a diffuse cost spread across everyone who buys things made of steel.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees in the spring of 2001, but none of them ever voted to advance it, and it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 1, 2001 and referred to the Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Education and the Workforce Committees.
It gathered 228 cosponsors — 181 of 208 House Democrats, 45 of 223 House Republicans, and both independents — a majority of the House.

It was referred to the Trade Subcommittee on March 8, the Domestic Monetary Policy Subcommittee on March 9, and the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on April 20, 2001 — and no further action was ever taken.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-importing manufacturers and their customers were better off, because they avoided quota-driven price increases and the new 1.5% steel tax, as were foreign steel exporters who kept their U.S. market access. Steelworkers and retirees, who had the broadest support in the House behind the bill, got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Peter Visclosky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors from steel-producing districts in both parties.

for.name: 181 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it overwhelming support from the Democratic side of the chamber.

for.name: 45 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors from steel-state districts such as Reps. Quinn, English, Ney, Hart, and Jones of Ohio.

against.name: Committee chairs of Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Education and the Workforce
against.role: Chairs of the three committees the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill stalled at the subcommittee referral stage for the life of the Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: The administration pursued import relief through its own trade-case process (a Section 201 safeguard investigation announced in 2001) rather than the bill's statutory quotas, and no action was taken on the bill in the Republican-controlled committees.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan and overwhelming — 181 of 208 House Democrats and 45 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored — so the bill's failure was not a party-line vote but a matter of the committees never acting.

industries.industry: Domestic steel, iron ore, and coke producers
industries.note: The bill would have locked in their market share with import quotas, handed them federally guaranteed loans, and paid their retiree health liabilities with a tax on all steel. Their gain came directly through higher steel prices for every steel-using business and household.
Quotas and the 1.5% excise tax would have raised their input costs, which they would pass on to consumers. These industries employ far more workers than steelmaking does.
The trust fund would have covered 75% of retiree health costs for plans serving retired and laid-off steelworkers, rescuing benefits abandoned by bankrupt companies.
Customs could refuse entry to any imports above pre-1997 monthly levels, cutting off much of their U.S. sales. Their cheaper steel was what steel buyers and consumers would lose access to.
